claims.text: Structural and chemical stability is governed by the interplay of atomic-scale diffusion, grain-boundary migration, and stable nanoscale precipitate formation.
Molecular dynamics simulations using machine-learning potentials can predict the governing stability processes.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloys have a uniform grain structure and a random elemental distribution.
Annealing at 800–1000 °C for 1–10 hours induces grain-boundary migration.
Annealing at 800–1000 °C for 1–10 hours promotes nanoscale precipitate formation.
An inert-gas or vacuum atmosphere prevents oxidation or contamination during high-temperature annealing.
Atomic-scale diffusion and grain-boundary migration lead to the formation of stable nanoscale precipitates.
Stable nanoscale precipitates enhance structural stability.
Stable nanoscale precipitates enhance chemical stability.
High-temperature annealing improves structural and chemical stability relative to an unannealed as-cast or as-synthesized baseline.
High-temperature annealing reduces grain growth relative to the unannealed baseline.
High-temperature annealing increases precipitate formation relative to the unannealed baseline.
High-temperature annealing enhances resistance to degradation relative to the unannealed baseline.
The prediction is limited to particular compositions, such as FeCoCrNi, and particular grain structures.
The prediction may not apply to other alloy systems or microstructures.
Failure of annealing to improve stability, including increased grain growth, reduced precipitate formation, or enhanced degradation, would falsify the hypothesis.
